works.label: The wharf named in the title brings the coast into the sphere of built commerce, while the etched lines make its structures and waters part of a dense working edge.

Charcoal and gouache turn a New York dock into a quick study of waterfront infrastructure. Made on the reverse of an advertisement, the drawing's support also links this harbor scene to circulation and exchange.
An eagle wharf is recorded through the spare, linear language of etching, locating the shoreline among piers and built structures rather than open beach.
Warehouses place storage and trade directly at the water's edge. The etching makes the Thames shore read as a constructed boundary, crowded by architecture.

The title identifies shipbuilding as the harbor's central activity, making the coast a site where vessels are made as well as launched. Its wood-engraved form reinforces the image's relation to print circulation and industrial labor.
Etching and drypoint attend to a smaller reach of Rotherhithe, where the riverbank is understood through its inhabited, working fabric.
Graphite reduces the lake shore to a direct, spare notation, shifting attention from built waterfront activity to the meeting of land and water.
A small overturned boat rests on sand before a distant pier and weathered structure. Its muted washes and low horizon hold the vessel in a quiet interval of abandonment rather than labor.
The New Jersey coast named in the title moves away from the dockside toward an exposed regional shoreline, where the coastal setting itself takes precedence.
Layered waves, reflective water, and a clouded sky spread across the page in pale washes. The shore nearly dissolves into this horizontal field of weather and sea.
Brown wash, blotting, and scraping give the rocky shore a dark, unsettled surface. Moonlight makes the coast a place shaped less by use than by rock, water, and nocturnal atmosphere.
Oyster boats place working vessels on the water, tying the coast to harvesting and transport. The photograph fixes that labor within the broad setting implied by the title.
In the Working Harbour, the wharf named in the title fixes the coast as built infrastructure, recorded through the tight black lines of etching.

A dock on New York’s North River places this drawing in the exhibition’s working zone, where the waterfront is defined by a site of mooring and exchange. Charcoal and gouache make the industrial subject notably immediate on the back of an advertisement.

Eagle Wharf adds another named landing place to the Working Harbour, treating the shore as a sequence of specific commercial edges. Its etched marks suit a scene structured by built surfaces and river traffic.
The title directs attention to warehouses, bringing storage and circulation into the harbour room. Etching reduces the Thames-side architecture to a network of dark linear forms.

Shipbuilding makes labor at the water’s edge the subject of this Working Harbour image. Reproduced as a wood engraving, it carries the activity of Gloucester Harbor into the graphic language of print circulation.
The Little Rotherhithe narrows the harbour’s scale from dockyard to a particular riverside place. Etching and drypoint give its working shoreline a rough, closely observed surface.
Oyster boats bring the exhibition’s harbor economy offshore, where vessels connect water, catch, and labor. The albumen print registers that trade through photography’s direct attention to the boats.
Lake Shore marks the turn to the Empty Shore, where a spare edge of water replaces the built harbor. Graphite keeps the scene reduced to shoreline and open space.

An overturned boat rests at the center of a sandy shore, no longer functioning as a working vessel. Muted watercolor washes, a low horizon, and the distant pier hold the scene between weathered remains and open water.

On the Coast of New Jersey shifts attention away from a named port to the broader coastal margin. In the Empty Shore, its title makes the coast itself the subject rather than the work conducted there.
Layered waves, reflective water, and a hazy, clouded sky leave the shoreline nearly empty of human activity. Soft washes fading into the paper make weather and horizon carry the image.
Moonlight turns the rocky coast into an interval of dark land, water, and sky. Brown wash, blotting, and scraping give the Empty Shore a worn, shifting surface.

Together the works ask how the same coast can be measured by human industry or by the vast intervals that remain when people recede.

works.label: The wharf named in the title fixes the coast at a working edge, where land meets the traffic of the river. Etching’s spare black lines suit this infrastructure of loading and departure.
A New York dock places the shoreline within a modern working city. Charcoal and gouache on the back of an advertisement make even the drawing’s support feel tied to commerce.
Another named wharf extends the exhibition’s sequence of riverfront labor. Its etched format reduces the built shore to a tight network of line.

Warehouses bring storage and trade to the water’s edge, making the coast an industrial boundary rather than an open prospect. The etching holds that dense architecture in a restrained range of black and white.
Shipbuilding makes the shore a place of construction, repair, and future passage. As a wood engraving published in 1873, the image carries that labor into reproducible print.
The title’s smaller place-name narrows the working riverfront to a local stretch of shore. Etching and drypoint keep its dockside world close to the grain of the paper.
The lake shore marks the exhibition’s turn away from docks and built infrastructure. Graphite pares the coast down to a direct, quiet record of edge and water.
A New Jersey coast shifts attention from the working harbor to the broader meeting of land and sea. Oil paint gives this quieter shoreline a sustained, slower field of observation.
Layered waves, reflective water, and a hazy sky leave the shore almost emptied of activity. Soft gray-green and beige washes let tide, weather, and distance take over.
Moonlight turns the rocky coast into a low-lit boundary of water, stone, and sky. Brown wash, blotting, and scraping make the scene feel shaped by shifting light rather than labor.
The boat named in the title has come to rest on the beach, no longer shown in transit or at work. Ink and wash place that pause within the exhibition’s quieter coastal stretch.
An overturned boat sits on sandy ground before a distant pier, holding traces of maritime use in a still scene. Muted watercolor and loose brushwork emphasize weathering, distance, and rest.

Together these works ask how the same strip of land can hold industry, solitude, and the recurring measure of tide.
